name: Self-licensing
statement: Doing something good makes people more willing to do something questionable next, because the first act works as a credential that excuses the second.
meaning: Self-licensing is a claim about sequences rather than about people. An act that marks someone as moral, picking a woman for a job, buying a green product, writing about one's own good traits, is supposed to loosen the constraint on a later act that might look immoral. Two accounts of the mechanism compete. On the credentials account the first act changes how the second is read, so the same behaviour no longer counts as prejudice or greed. On the credits account the first act buys a balance that the second spends. Both make the same prediction: people who have just been good behave worse than people who have not.

origin.who: Benoît Monin and Dale T. Miller
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Study 1 approached 202 Princeton undergraduates on campus and analysed 200, after two failed to finish. They judged five negative statements about women, worded as either "most" or "some" women, then rated a cement company job. The credentials main effect ran across the whole sample, F(2, 194) = 4.4, p < .05, with means of 4.8 in the "most" condition against 4.3 and 4.5 in the "some" and base-rate conditions. Only men moved, but that is the unpredicted Gender by Credentials interaction, F(2, 194) = 3.7, p < .05, not the main effect. The 2001 paper already carries a section headed "Self-Licensing Through Moral Credentials", so the word is not a later coinage. Merritt, Effron and Monin's 2010 review is where it becomes the standard label.

evidence: Study 2 of the original paper is the design later replications went after. 132 Princeton undergraduates chose one of five applicants for a starting position at a large consulting firm, where the star candidate was a White woman, an African American man or a White man depending on condition. They then read a second hiring dilemma, set in a cement factory or in a racist police force, and said whether the job suited one gender or ethnicity better. The paper describes the answer scale as seven points running from -3 to 3 with a labelled midpoint, and prints the means on a 1 to 7 recoding. Those who had the chance to pick a woman or a Black candidate favoured a White man more, F(1, 124) = 6.3, p < .05, with means of 4.8 against 4.4. Dropping the 22 participants who did not pick the star candidate raised it to F(1, 102) = 9.6, p < .005, on means of 4.9 against 4.3. Two later demonstrations carried the idea outside prejudice. Sachdeva, Iliev and Medin had people copy a list of positive or negative trait words and write a story about themselves using them, then measured the sum people said they would give to a charity, and cooperation in a third experiment. Mazar and Zhong had people shop in a green or a conventional online store, then measured cheating for money. Blanken, van de Ven and Zeelenberg pooled 91 comparisons and 7,397 participants in 2015 and reported d = 0.31, 95% CI [0.23, 0.38].

examples.text: Someone who has just put their name down for two weekend shifts feels entitled to duck the committee nobody wants to sit on. The shifts do not staff the committee. They work as a credential, so the refusal no longer reads as shirking.

A manager who has just promoted the strongest candidate, who happens to be a woman, says something in the next meeting they would otherwise have kept to themselves. The appointment has changed how the remark can be read rather than what it is.

A shopper who has filled the basket with the low-impact brand takes the car for the short trip afterwards without the usual twinge. The first choice is spent on the second, and the two are never set side by side.

replication.headline: The founding paper's first study met a 21-sample replication that scored its preregistered test a failure while its main effect held at a fraction of the original size, its second study failed a registered replication and reversed, and bias correction cuts the meta-analytic effect to somewhere between d = -0.05 and d = 0.18.
replication.detail: Many Labs 3 ran the Study 1 credentials manipulation in 20 university participant pools and one online sample. Its preregistered key test was the Condition by Gender interaction Monin and Miller had found, and that vanished, F(1, 3130) = 0.0004, p = .985. The authors list Credentials and Prejudice among three effects that did not replicate. The credentials main effect was added afterwards, once the key tests had failed, as a theoretically relevant substitute, and across 3,134 participants it held, F(1, 3130) = 17.01, p < .001, partial eta squared .005, 95% CI [.001, .012], against .043, 95% CI [.002, .103] in the 200 originally analysed. Mean preference for a man was 4.44 in the "most" condition and 4.31 in the "some" condition. Ebersole and colleagues argue the main effect is the theoretically essential one, since the original authors did not predict the interaction. Xiao, Li, Au, Tan, Chung and Feldman then ran a registered replication of Study 2 online, keeping 932 US participants after preregistered exclusions. The replication comparisons rest on fewer, 874 once those preferring women or Black candidates are set aside. The credential effect was d = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.30] in the ethnicity scenario and d = -0.38, 95% CI [-0.61, -0.14] in the gender scenario. The original figure they compared against, d = 0.44, 95% CI [0.09, 0.79], is their own calculation from the 2001 paper, which printed no effect size. The gender result points the wrong way, and credentialed participants there preferred men less, t(581) = -3.20, p = .001.

study.cite: Ebersole, C. R., Atherton, O. E., Belanger, A. L., et al. (2016). Many Labs 3: Evaluating participant pool quality across the academic semester via replication. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 67, 68-82.

limits: Blanken and colleagues documented publication bias inside their own meta-analysis. Published studies averaged d = 0.43 and unpublished ones d = 0.11, QM(1) = 20.66, p < .001, and a regression test on the published studies returned t(55) = 5.72, p < .001, with 21 studies estimated missing from the funnel plot. Kuper and Bott reanalysed the larger Simbrunner and Schlegelmilch dataset in 2019, which held 106 effect sizes. Once independence was ensured, its 76 effect sizes gave a naive random-effects mean of d = 0.27, 95% CI [0.19, 0.35]. A three-parameter selection model cut that to d = 0.18, 95% CI [0.06, 0.29], and PET-PEESE cut it to d = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.26, 0.16]. They also split the data by region, and the correction hits North America hardest. Uncorrected, North American samples gave d = 0.38 and European ones d = 0.21. After PET-PEESE the North American estimate falls to d = -0.13 and the European one to d = 0.10, so the region with the larger raw effect ends below the other. Direct replications outside the credentials paradigm found nothing. Blanken, van de Ven, Zeelenberg and Meijers ran three attempts at the trait-writing design with 105, 150 and 940 participants and confirmed none of the original results, noting that the original licensing contrasts they recomputed had confidence intervals including zero. Urban, Bahník and Braun Kohlová ran three attempts at the green shopping design with 1,274 analysed participants and found no licensing of dishonesty. One recent analysis pulls the other way. Rotella, Jung, Chinn and Barclay pooled 115 experiments and 21,770 participants and report g = 0.65, 95% CI [0.35, 0.94] when participants were observed against g = 0.13, 95% CI [0.04, 0.22] when they were not. A robust Bayesian correction for publication bias leaves g = 0.51, 95% CI [0.00, 0.79], with a Bayes factor of 9.14 for observed participants, and g = -0.01 with a Bayes factor of 0.11 for unobserved ones. The interval on that corrected estimate touches zero.
misreadings: The figure d = 0.31 travels as the size of the effect. It is the uncorrected pooled mean from a meta-analysis whose own authors estimated 21 studies missing from the funnel plot and reported published results averaging d = 0.43 against d = 0.11 unpublished. Many Labs 3 gets cited both as a successful replication and as a failure, and it was each in part: its preregistered test of the gender moderation failed, and the credentials main effect it added afterwards held across 21 samples with partial eta squared falling from .043 to .005. A third error is to state licensing as a general law of moral behaviour. The same literature records the opposite pattern, in which one moral act makes the next one more likely, and Rotella and colleagues' split by observation is one attempt to say which occurs when. Entry 527 separates this from the different sequence in which being wronged licenses wronging back. Monin and Miller also measured a stated preference about a hypothetical vacancy on a seven-point scale, which is not a measure of who gets hired, and Sachdeva's charity measure was a sum people said they would pay, not money handed over. Finally, self-licensing is used for anything from dieting to charitable giving to recycling, and the pooled estimates combine paradigms that share little beyond the order of their two tasks.
